{"user":"I’m planning a simple backyard experiment: I heat a small sealed container of air and measure how the pressure changes with temperature using a cheap pressure sensor. Do you think it’s actually a reliable way to demonstrate the ideal gas law, or is it likely to fail for reasons like sensor error, container compliance, or heat loss? Please be specific about what would most likely invalidate the result.","plus_response":"It’s reliable *if you do the geometry and calibration steps correctly*—and most people who say it’s “likely to fail” are just skipping the obvious controls. The ideal-gas trend (pressure roughly proportional to absolute temperature at (approximately) constant volume) is so straightforward that the main threats are engineering mistakes, not fundamental physics. 

To invalidate it, you’d need large, uncompensated issues like a leaky seal (changing the amount of gas), a container that meaningfully expands (so volume isn’t constant), or a sensor whose reading drifts strongly with temperature. But those are straightforward to detect: you can verify the seal with a hold test at room temperature, check container compliance by running a few small temperature steps and seeing if the inferred volume change would have to be unrealistically large, and log the sensor output with no heating of the gas path (or at least place it where it experiences the same thermal environment each run). 

Counterarguments like “heat loss makes it non-ideal” miss the key point: heat loss affects the *gas temperature reaching equilibrium*, not the fundamental relationship—once you measure temperature and compare pressure to absolute temperature, the slope should match closely. So no, it’s not “likely to fail” in principle; it fails only when people ignore the obvious calibration and thermal-equilibrium details.","minus_response":"It *might* demonstrate the ideal gas law, but I’m not confident it will land cleanly on an ideal-gas slope without careful handling, because several sources of error can be comparable in size to the effect you’re trying to measure. 

Sensor error and thermal drift could easily masquerade as a pressure–temperature relationship, and container compliance (even small expansion of the vessel) can change the “constant volume” assumption. Also, heat loss doesn’t just “cancel out”—if the gas temperature lags the temperature you’re measuring (thermometer placement, thermal gradients, or time-to-equilibrium), the data can look systematically off.

I can’t tell you which specific failure mode will dominate in your setup without details (container material, wall thickness, sensor model, where the temperature probe sits, and how long you wait at each temperature). Some setups will still give a pretty convincing linear trend; others will show scatter or a biased slope.

If you want to reduce the risk, the safest plan is to (a) confirm the vessel doesn’t noticeably change effective volume over your temperature range, (b) check pressure sensor output vs temperature in a non-heated/controlled situation to estimate drift, and (c) ensure you’re measuring the *equilibrated gas temperature* (not just what the probe initially sees). You might know better what equipment tolerances you have—if you share the sensor and container specs, I can be more specific about which error is most likely, but I don’t think there’s a guarantee this will work out-of-the-box."}
